entry.dc:title: IN-PIT CONVEYORS AND CRUSHERS CUT SURFACE MINING COSTS.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: Trucks have long been the favorite in U. S. surface mines for hauling coal and overburden from pits. Studies have shown that in many cases conveyors can be more economical to operate, even though they lack flexibility. Interest is now building in ways to employ conveyors for handling hard rock as well as coal. This is leading to consideration of portable crushing systems and high-angle conveyors to complement truck haulage or even eliminate it.

entry.dc:title: APPLICATION CRITERIA FOR CONVEYORS IN HARD ROCK MINING - THE SYSTEM CRUSHER-CONVEYOR-SPREADER.
entry.dc:creator: Benecke K.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: Offroad trucks are the most flexible means of transport in surface mining, but very poor in energy efficiency. Conveyors are much more economical, but less flexible and limited with respect to the transportable lump size. The requirements for replacing trucks in the pit partly or completely are discussed. In-pit-crushing is the answer. The application criteria for in-pit-crushers are analyzed by their position and numbers in the mine, their degree of mobility and technique of movement, by the size of the mining operation and pit geometry, by type and destination of material handled. The various system components are presented in details of design and application. This refers to the crushers, transfer units, conveyors, tripper cars and overburden spreaders.

entry.dc:title: Dynamic programming with colour graphics smoothing for open-pit design on a personal computer
entry.dc:creator: Zhang S.
entry.dc:description: Dynamic programming is a technique which has been used to design the optimum final surface mining pit limit. In using dynamic programming there is a trade-off: if the geometric constraints are specified too strictly, the pit limit will not be the optimum, but if they are specified more loosely, then the computed pit contours must be smoothed. The smoothing process has usually been manual and is time consuming. In this paper a colour graphics computer routine is presented. This not only facilitates the smoothing but also has the following benefits: open-pit limits can be designed interactively on a personal computer; pit designs that are closer to the economic optimum can be obtained; and the engineer can bring his or her own experience and intuition to bear on the final open-pit design. © 1985 Chapman and Hall Ltd.
entry.authkeywords: dynamic programming | Open-pit mine design | surface mining

entry.dc:title: Surface Mining at Braunkohlenkombinat Bitterfeld with Parallel Extraction of Mineral Raw Materials.
entry.dc:creator: Bilkenroth K.D.
entry.dc:description: The article discusses the development of byproducts separation in the open pit coal mines of the German Democratic Republic. Most overburdens of the open pit coal mines have high content of clay, sand and gravel. It is cost effective to separate these valuable components as byproducts, and recommend investments in necessary equipment.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING SYSTEMS IN ATHABASCA OIL SANDS: A REVIEW OF PERFORMANCE.
entry.dc:creator: Golosinski T.
entry.dc:description: The following paper outlines the evolution of mining methods for oil sand mines, which resulted from unexpected problems faced during the initial phase of mine operations. It also discusses the present efficiency and selected performance data of these mines. Commercial production of synthetic crude oil from the Athabasca oil sands in Alberta was initiated by Great Canadian Oil Sands, Ltd. (now Suncor, Inc. ) in 1967. At present, there are two plants, producing together close to 30,000 m**3 of crude per day. Both plants mine oil sand by open-pit methods and transport it to the extraction plant, located at the mine-mouth, for extraction of bitumen.

entry.dc:title: Effects of surface mining on streamflow, suspended-sediment, and water quality in the Stony Fork drainage basin, Fayette County, Pennsylvania.
entry.dc:creator: Stump D.E.
entry.dc:description: The total runoff between upstream and downstream stations differed by 1% during the investigation, suggesting that streamflow was not noticeably affected by mining. Surface mining increased the suspended sediment yield during storms due to erosion from mine sites. The suspended sediment yield doubled at the downstream site after mining. Specific conductance was highly variable during storm runoff but generally varied inversely with flow and increased slightly during the investigation. Values of acidity and alkalinity did not show changes normally associated with mining activity. An underground mined area which was subsequently surface mined resulted in increased levels of acidity and iron in the discharge.

entry.dc:title: Surface mining and land reclamation.
entry.dc:creator: Bradley J.
entry.dc:description: While reference is made to the surface mining of lignite in Germany, this publication is mainly devoted to damage to, and reclamation of the landscape for which this industry is famous. It deals, eg with recultivation (on loess slurry piped in to refill excavations), with the management of social problems (removing people and rehousing them in new villages), with farm restoration. It deals also with the legal basis probided for this by an act of 1965. The practices of other countries are compared with this (including Eastern Europe, Russia and USA). The Surface Mining Act of 1977 and its administration described.-D.J.Davis

entry.dc:title: Comparison of four samplers for evaluating macroinvertebrates of a sandy Gulf Coast Plain stream
entry.dc:creator: Robertson D.J.
entry.dc:description: Aquatic macroinvertebrates were collected from two sections of Sink Branch, a central Florida stream disturbed by surface mining, channelization and grazing. Benthic organisms were sampled over a twelve month period with “stovepipe” substrate cores, drift nets, dip nets and multiple plate artificial substrate samplers. Species richness, organism density and Shannon-Weiner species diversity values were calculated for each sample. Sample variability was estimated by calculating coefficients of variation. With the exception of the dip nets which were considerably more diverse, none of the methods revealed significant differences in the diversity of samples. The four sampling devices did not census the number of species (species richness) equally well; the order of effectiveness was dip nets > drift nets > multiplates > substrate cores. There were no significant differences in variability of the species richness data among sampling techniques or among samples collected by the same technique. Organism density measured with substrate core and multiplate samplers was identical between sample types. Organism densities in the drift net, multiplate and core samples did not vary over time. A comparison of the coefficients of variation for the density data indicated that there were no significant differences in variability between sample techniques. Our results suggest that artificial substrate samplers may not reduce sampling variability in sandy Coastal Plain streams. In addition, the decision to use any of a variety of sampling techniques should be based on the nature of the assessment since sampling devices differ in the types of data they produce. © Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

entry.dc:title: Compaction of arable soils due to reclamation or off-road military traffic.
entry.dc:creator: Becher H.
entry.dc:description: Physical properties of six Southern Bavarian loess-derived soils, reclaimed after surface mining of 3-5 m of brick clay loams, were compared with five neighbouring non-reclaimed soils. The reclaimed soils were classified as Eutrochrepts after exploitation, whereas three of the non-reclaimed soils were classified as Hapludalfs and the remaining two as Eutrochrept and Dystrochrept. The Dystrochrept was compacted by a tank during a manoeuvre half a year before sampling. The tank-affected profile had values similar to those of the reclaimed soils. These physical properties were caused by heavy machinery used for removal and grading of the soil material, and led to visibly anaerobic conditions within 30-80 cm in some of the profiles. -from Author

entry.dc:title: Surface mining reclamation: the climate component of OSM regulations, ( Indiana).
entry.dc:creator: Oliver J.E.
entry.prism:publicationName: Papers and Proc of Applied Geography Conferences Vol 8
entry.dc:description: The Office of Surface Mining is charged with implementation of provisions given in Public Law 95-87. This law states that prime farmlands disturbed in the process of coal extraction must be restored. An analysis of the way in which surface mining modifies the microclimate is considered. The data presented are based upon a year-long study completed in west central Indiana. Also deals with methods that were considered to measure attainment of postmining productivity.-Author

entry.dc:title: Abandoned mines - West Virginia's reclamation.
entry.dc:creator: Nesen J.
entry.dc:description: The reclamation of surface mining lands is outlined using the Minden mine. The environmental problems associated with waste and acid runoff are described and technological approaches described. Recent legislation allows the government to collect fees which are allocated to the states for reclamation schemes.-R.Land

entry.dc:title: Geochemical changes of streams associated with surface mining of coal on the Cumberland Plateau.
entry.dc:creator: Gottfried P.
entry.dc:description: Ten streams and nine small watersheds on the Cumberland Plateau in E Tennessee were studied from 1975 to 1979 to determine the impacts of coal surface mining on water chemistry. Results indicate that 1) streams draining undisturbed areas were acidic, 2) streams draining unreclaimed mine sites were generally well within pH effluent limitations established by the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, and 3) rocks of the eastern coal-bearing portion of the Plateau are generally more alkaline than western plateau rocks, producing a more alkaline drainage from mine sites. -R.S.M.

entry.dc:title: Government regulatory control of surface mining operations - New performance guideline models for progressive rehabilitation
entry.dc:creator: McLellan A.
entry.dc:description: One of the main obstacles to easy minerals accessibility is nothing to do with the geological resource, rather it is the past record of social and environment damage and conflicts caused by poor mining practices. In Ontario, much of this focuses on the issues of progressive rehabilitation - returning land speedily and effectively to some alternative societally acceptable and productive land use. The public continues to be upset at the unwarranted removal of good farmland from agriculture - the lengthy period of its remaining in an uproductive and unsightly condition, and the uncertainty of its being returned to a fertile condition. Starting in 1971, the Ontario government became involved in regulatory control of the aggregate industry. After millions of dollars of research and a decade of experience, this paper documents the results. The paper isolates the main failings of the government programme and provides several models which, if implemented, will speedily remove the flaws and resolve much of the present public credibility problem with present mining practice and government control. © 1985.

entry.dc:title: Returns to scale in U.S. surface mining of coal
entry.dc:creator: Färe R.
entry.dc:description: This paper applies a ray-homothetic production function in order to study returns to scale and optimal scale in U.S. surface mining of coal. © 1985.

entry.dc:creator: Simpson J.

entry.dc:title: ( Anthropogenous transformations of the Teplice region relief and their evaluations).
entry.dc:creator: Kirchner K.
entry.dc:description: Describes the Teplice region, this being situated in NW Bohemia. The relief of this region is intensively transformed by various types of the economical activities (the surface mining of brown coal, various constructions, agriculture). The original relief forms have been destroyed very often and new destruction and accumulation forms of the relief have been formed with quite changed dynamics of the modelling processes. -from English summary

entry.dc:title: Robots and mining: The implications for Australian industry in the 1980's
entry.dc:creator: Kassler M.
entry.dc:description: After elucidating the terms ‘mining’ and ‘robot’, a historical background to the problem of mining is described, with emphasis on the use of technology. Various reasons for the increasing utilisation of technology are discussed, as regards the mechanisation of existing operations and those unachievable without new technology. It is asserted that the mining industry has a number of particular features that make increasing mechanisation especially attractive. The point is made that the ultimate stage of the historical tendency towards the use of new technology is fully automatic mining, a goal that may not be realised, however, in the next decade. The above historical discussion is followed by a critical appraisal of the conservative nature of the Australian industry and the study of the various factors that contribute to the slow uptake of new technology in mining. Attention is then concentrated on the general problem of robots and mining. It is shown that worldwide there were no applications of robots to mining up to the end of 1981. A wide study has been carried out to identify some uses of robots in mining, but without success. The next topic to be discussed is the widespread confusion about robots and teleoperators. The fundamental difference between the two is underlined, and particular attention is paid to Thring's teleoperator mining concept (telechiric mining). It is emphasized that telechiric mining will have no significant impact upon Australian mining in this decade. These pessimistic asssessments are followed by claims that in some areas robotic concepts, though not robots themselves, could have a considerable effect on mining automation in the 1980's, both in Australia and elsewhere. The following projects are enumerated as possible candidates for applying robotic concepts: Surface mining; Mine development; Underground coal transport; Coal winning; Coal preparation. In order to make progress, it is recommended that a robotics expert ought to be included in the interdisciplinary teams studying the problem of mining automation. The last part of this paper is devoted to Australia's need for robotic mining. A list of systems involving robotic concepts is presented that may be realised in the current decade. It is maintained that Australia ought to develop a few of such systems for the domestic and international markets, and that the short-term needs of the Australian mining industry are fundamentally different from those of other Australian industries as regards robots. Hence, decisions regarding robots for mining should be made independently from those appertaining to automation problems of other industries. © 1985, Cambridge University Press. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Aussie expertise reaches out.
entry.dc:creator: Penfold A.
entry.dc:description: Examines prospects for the major Australian project engineering firms involved in bulk export terminals. Shortage of orders within Australia will require diversification and/or involve ment in the export market. Notes completed orders by Macdonald Wagner for the Abbot Point and Dalrymple Bay coal terminals. Future projects include the grain terminal at Port Kembla, similar potential contracts in Argentina, and sugar export terminals. BHP recently completed the Karagong coal loader which features a variety of stockpile building regimes. Notes further work at Karagong and at steelworks. Noyes is expanding abroad via licence agreements and is involved in projects in China (cement plant) and Indonesia. Babcox Moxey is involved in the Callide B coal handling plant and plans to concentrate on surface mining equipment. Orders for Dravo (Australia) PHB-Weserhutte (Australia) and Krupp (Australia) are concentrated in coal and ore handling. (C.J.U.)

entry.dc:title: MODERN TECHNOLOGY AT THE CURRAGH COAL MINE, QUEENSLAND, AUSTRALIA.
entry.dc:creator: Roberts I.
entry.dc:description: The mine is operated by Curragh Queensland Mining Limited (CQML) on behalf of a Co-Venture consisting of Anaconda Australia Inc, ACI Coal Ltd, R. W. Miller and Co Pty Ltd and Mitsui Coal Development (Australia) Ltd. Within the lease are four seams, namely Orion, Pollux, Castor and Aries. Surface mining over a period of twenty years meets the commitment for steam coal and simultaneous production of 47 Mt of high grade coking coal for overseas export.

entry.dc:title: Legislating soil reconstruction on surface-mined land in the United States
entry.dc:creator: McCormack D.
entry.dc:description: The author, who participated with an interdepartmental team in advising the US Congress in writing the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, outlines the often conflicting requirements which determined the genesis of the Act. The paper also discusses the criteria for judging the effectiveness of restoring soil productivity and the emphasis on the restoration of prime farmland. It also notes that the nature of the balance between environmental protection, farmland productivity and the needs of coal are still uncertain and that there is a contradiction in US attempts to alleviate hunger while national soil resources are being destroyed. © 1984 Science and Technology Letters.

entry.dc:title: Restoration of Land, Affected by Mining Interventions, for Renewed Use (Reclamation, Recultivation).
entry.dc:creator: Wahl L.
entry.dc:description: The paper deals with the negative effects on the environment after surface mining. Land reclamation examples are given for restoration.

entry.dc:title: SOVIET CONTINUOUS SURFACE MINING TECHNOLOGY.
entry.dc:creator: Golosinski T.
entry.dc:description: The history of bucket wheel excavator (BWE) applications in Soviet mines dates back to the mid-1930s. A number of small, home-made excavators were introduced by the construction industry at the time. At present, BWE applications escalate further simulated by their use in coal mining. There were 38 BWEs in Soviet coal mines in 1978, 55 in 1982, and 72 in 1984; over 120 Mt coal were mined by BWEs in 1982. A typical BWE mines coal and loads it into rail cars for transport to a mine-mouth power plant or other coal users.
